subtopic: MONOPOLISTIC TRADE RESTRICTIONS-COMBINATIONS IN RESTRAINT OF TRADE

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) :. moved for leave to introduce bill No. 193, to amend the Combines Investigation Act.
He said: This bill arises from the report "Canada and International Cartels" which was tabled during the course of the last session and which was prepared by the special committee under the commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act. Hon. members will recall that the report illustrated the undesirable effects on the Canadian economy of the operations of private international trade combinations known as cartels, and generally the obstacle to full employment in either the international or the domestic sphere, which might result from undue restraints of trade. It recommended consideration by the government of certain lines of approach with reference to the forthcoming international discussions respecting international trade. It also recommended that steps be taken both legisla-

Questions
tively and administratively to make the Combines Investigation Act more effective in preventing and removing undesirable domestic restraints of trade and in obtaining and making available for the determining of government policy information respecting the effects of international cartels on the Canadian economy.
The principal steps to implement the report require no legislation but merely larger staff and appropriations for the commission, and that will be dealt with when the estimates of the department are being considered by the house. Legislation is necessary, however, to remove certain anomalies from the present act and to provide the necessary tools for the revived activities of the commission.
The bill proposes no changes in the definitions of offences or in the basic scheme of the act. It provides for greater flexibility in the administration of the act and removes or modifies some of the restrictions on the operations of the act which were added in 1935 and 1937 when the dominion trade and industry commission was set up, and it proposes to restore to the commission some of the activities that were entrusted to the dominion trade and industry commission, under the original set-up of that body which was to control the Combines Investigation Act administration. That was removed in 1937 and the amendments proposed in this bill are with respect to procedure and not with respect to the substance of the offences aimed at by the legislation.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

The house resumed from Tuesday, June 4, consideration in committee of bill No. 155, respecting the operation of government companies-Mr. Howe-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 8-Employment and remuneration of officers and servants.

subsubtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose last night we were discussing security checks in respect of employees of crown corporations. I had referred to a reply given by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to a similar question I had put to him when we were discussing the atomic energy bill. At page 2123 the minister's reply is reported in this way:
For several years every man or woman who has been employed by the National Research Council has been screened by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
In the interval since last night I have checked the records of the employees of the public service and others who are now accused of espionage and are undergoing trial. I find nearly all of them were employed after the beginning of the war. It seems to me that since two of them were employed by crown companies, this is a point which the house ought not to overlook; the government must have some control over appointments made by directors of crown companies and should check their security categories. I think that contention is also supported by what occurs in other realms of government employment. An item appeared in the press to-day with reference to the remarks made in a committee by that "able and tireless civil servant, Mr. Hume Wrong. When asked whether the Department of External Affairs had any check on the security or political affiliations of its employees, Mr. Wrong stated he thought it would be unfair to investigate the political affiliations of any applicant. That had to do with the civil service, this has to do with people who will be engaged to work for crown companies.

Go vern ment Companies
I would not want to be misunderstood on this issue, because I have in mind the unfortunate circumstances that have developed since last February when this whole business of espionage broke upon the Canadian people. Just to keep the record straight I should like to quote two items from the first interim report of the royal commission. In the first interim report issued on March 2, 1946, the justices report:
The evidence establishes that a network of under-cover agents has been organized and developed for the purpose of obtaining secret and confidential information particularly from employees of departments and agencies of the dominion government.
I should like to quote from the second interim report, issued on March 14, as follows:
In a case of this nature where the evidence has revealed the existence of an organization constituting at least a threat to the safety and interests of the state, as evidenced by the fact that some witnesses holding strategic positions have made the significant statement under oath that they had a loyalty which took priority over the loyalty owed by them to their own country, and for that reason they acted as they did, and would unquestionably have continued so to act had they not been detected.
In to-day's paper there is an editorial dealing with a speech made by the national leader of the Labour Progressive party. In that speech the leader of that party tore away the veil which previously covered the motives of the party when he said:
We want 10,000 new members this year. We want a mass marxist party-a party of communists.
That is what was said in Toronto at a meeting held on June 2. The fact is that both in government departments and in crown companies there have been people employed who have professed a greater loyalty to another ideology than toward their own country. The minister has said that they have been checking on the affiliations and beliefs of these people for several years, but that answer is inadequate, because nearly all these people who have been reported as haying engaged in espionage work were employed by the government since the beginning of the war. We are dealing with Eldorado and Dominion Arsenals; in both these companies employees will have access to official information and secret processes which might be turned against this country, against the empire, or against the United States. Therefore there should be a greater check on all empolyees of crown companies.

subsubtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
To reply first to the question *as to what precautions were taken, all direct employees of the department of Munitions and Supply and all direct employees of the national
research council were finger-printed and their records explored by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Reports were rendered to the department in all doubtful cases, and certain men left the employ of the department on that account. So far as employees of crown companies are concerned, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were in charge of that work. The record of each employee was checked if he had access to any information of importance. However, with all the precautions that can be taken. I know of no way in which the government can assure itself that a man who enters the service of a department with a stainless reputation cannot be seduced by communism or some other allegiance. When a man is hired, there is no way in which we can predict with certainty what his course will be in the yearn to follow.

Under section 8 of the bill wide powers are being given to the company and its officials in the employment of servants, agents and officers. With an ordinary company that would only be proper. Last night I suggested to the minister that he should consider putting under the Civil Service Act all employees who render services similar to those rendered by civil servants. I would except expert and specially skilled personnel, scientists, et cetera, so far as salaries and wages are concerned. Antogonism will'be created among our regularly emploj'ed civil servants if government employees in crown companies are employed under different conditions or circumstances. There will be a large number of employees in these crown companies with qualifications and abilities similar to those in the regular civil service, and there should be no great differentiation between the treatment given to these people and that given to the members of the government service who are appointed through the civil service commission.
This point is particularly emphasized by the powers that are given to the governor in council to advance moneys to crown corporations for operating expenses and capital investments, to the tune of one-half million dollars as a maximum at any one time, and an additional total of one-half million dollars in any one fiscal year-and I believe that can be done in every fiscal year-for the extension and improvement of plant, the purchase of capital stock, et cetera. A thorough study of the bill will disclose that the governor in council can take out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund any amounts within those limitations that they see fit to take without submitting them to parliament, the minister has stated that they will be sub-

If this money were not coming out of the public treasury but were being paid by some private enterprise, it would be no concern of mine. But I am objecting to the wide powers of expenditure of public money which these directors have. That is the whole basis of my argument. The directors and officers of the companies can hire anybody, from low-paid clerks and stenographers to highly-paid scientists, engineers, experts and managers, and can fix the rates of compensation without reference to parliament and without any regard to the scale of salaries paid to similar employees in the civil service, whose salaries and con-
ditions of emplojmient are determined by the Civil Service Act and regulations. Here we have the public treasury contributing a substantial portion of the working capital of these companies, and the directors being given almost unlimited powers to hire their employees at whatever salaries they see fit, without parliament having any say in the matter. This is definitely blank cheque legislation and uncontrolled expenditure. It is therefore ail the more important that the employees of the crown companies should have their terms of employment and compensation governed by the Civil Service Act.
I am not so sure that the minister himself has appreciated what is involved, because in answer to a question of mine he stated yesterday, at page 2182 of Hansard:
They can be appropriated only by vote of parliament. My hon. friend is right. They must be appropriated by vote of parliament or otherwise refunded.
With that I agree, if we look upon the passing of this bill as a voting by parliament. But I submit that if we pass the bill in its present form the directors and officers have the right to hire anybody they like and pay them what salaries they like, and get the money required by order in council or upon recommendation of the minister from unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund. All that is to be done without the sanction of parliament, other than what is given in the bill itself. Therefore if we pass this section and other sections in their present form parliament will be divesting itself of any authority or power over the hiring of the employees of these companies and the terms and conditions of their employment, even though they are all being paid substantially at the public expense. Parliament should not divest itself of the power of scrutinizing appropriations and of passing estimates for this purpose; we should retain control from year to year of the expenditure of public moneys by the directors or management of these crown companies. If we pass the bill in its present form we are breaking all custom in that we shall be, first of all, establishing a separate set of government employees who will not be working under the same terms and conditions as those in the regular civil service who have proven themselves loyal, efficient and competent; and secondly we are allowing the directors of these crown companies-perhaps scientists, engineers, businessmen-to expend moneys out of consolidated revenue without parliament having the right to scrutinize the expenditures before they are made. The minister was technically right when- he said last night that appropria-

tions made to these crown companies appear in the estimates; nevertheless they appear as statutory enactments.

I felt when I was raising the point last night that possibly I was not as sure of my ground as I should be, but I found great consolation when I saw from the minister's answers that he was just as uncertain as I was. Will the minister stand up and say now that the appropriations for these government companies will be passed as ordinary estimates are passed before the expenditures are made? Parliament has no check on expenditures if it is allowed to review them only after they are made. That is not business. That is not the way government should be carried on. Parliament should have the right to scrutinize particulars of the proposed expenditures and have a full discussion just as we do on the ordinary estimates. The ones I have mentioned are recent. That is why I mentioned them. I mentioned them because my hon. friends voted for them and I thought the matter would be fresh in their minds. The practice
of government companies employing people outside the Civil Service Act is not new. It was done in the dim and distant past, when my hon. friends were in power. It was done in the case Sf the Canadian National railways. Every employee of the Canadian National railways is employed by the management, and his salary is paid by the management. My hon. friends voted for it. Hon. gentlemen are trying to suggest that we are breaking new ground. This is not so in any particular. We are following established practice in connection with government-owned companies. There is no government company that employs its men through the civil service commission, nor has there been one over the years. As a matter, of fact, in the employment of tradesmen, for instance, the practice in government companies is exactly the same as that followed by the civil service commission. Tradesmen employed by the government through the civil service commission receive prevailing rates; the prevailing rate in the district is established by the Minister of Labour, and the employees are paid that rate. The practice is exactly the same as in crown companies. There is the additional protection, however, that almost all the employees of crown companies are organized and have contracts with one of the international unions, and they have the right to bargain between management and labour.
I cannot think of any reason why we should argue the matter at greater length. I repeat, we have followed the established practice, and it seems to me that every safeguard is provided in the crown companies referred to. The same provision is made in this act as in those establishing other crown companies, and I would point out that the employees in crown companies outnumber all civil servants by at least two to one and perhaps three to one. I think that explanation should be sufficient.

subsubtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Involved in section 8 is an important principle to which I would direct the attention of the minister. We had an experience with two other corporations in connection with the questions of employment control and wages, and there we saw the House of Commons divesting itself of control over these two corporations. The minister is himself an able engineer. I can remember when he was a younger man practising his profession, and he is fully aware of conditions governing the employment of men in his profession. As far as possible I would like to see him give a preference to the graduates of our Canadian universities when it comes to employing technical men under this bill. This
Government Companies

is the golden month of commencement in the universities of Canada, and there is no part of science that is more the child of science, the bright-eyed creature of science, than the engineering profession.
As the minister knows, between the two great wars we lost thousands of our young graduates to the United States-graduates in medicine, physics, chemistry and in other branches of science, who went south and contributed to the development of that country. After the first great war, 1,250,(XX) Canadians went to the United States, as was indicated in a survey that was tabled in this house. Many of those men fought for this country at the risk of their lives. I hope therefore the minister will see to it that as far as possible graduates from our Canadian universities are given the preference in employment with crown companies.
I know it will be said that this corporation will make its annual report to the directors and that the facts will be submitted to parliament. Well, we had great hopes in that regard from the Canadian National, and we were also promised great things in connection with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I remember the stand which my former leader took, quite properly, in regard to that corporation. He insisted that they should report to the house. But what do we find to-day? If you want to find anything about employment or control or salaries, for instance, they will tell you nothing.
The Chippewa canal, developing 550,000 horsepower, was built by graduates of Canadian universities. Sir Adam Beck insisted that the engineers engaged in that great undertaking should be Canadians, from Canadian universities. Canadians were employed and they built that magnificent system. As I said before, the minister was engaged in his profession as a young man at the time I was chairman of the harbour board, and he knows the record of Canadian graduates in discoveries in the northwest territories and the development of mining and other engineering projects in Canada. Only the other day I was making inquiries as to where the graduates in engineering of the university of Toronto and other universities will go to make a living, and I was told about what they had done in the great mining development in new Ontario-gold, silver, zinc, platinum, copper, lead, in fact, thirty-six minerals. Survey parties from Toronto, McGill, Queen's and other universities across Canada went out as students, and later as engineers, exploring these fields, and at times they had with them high school students. These people did not 
ask for any easy job in the summer time; they did not work forty hours a week, because you can never develop the resources of the country in that way. They left as students an easy time in the city and worked hard in the holidays to do something for this country.
I hope that the directors of these crown companies will consider this question of employment in the light of what I have said, because we are removing the corporation from the control of parliament and of the civil service commission. I hope it may work out all right; no one knows. I can say that I never got a job for anyone through the civil service commission from the time they were appointed. You cannot even get a branch subpost office where it is badly needed.
Coming back to section 8, I am not one of those who believe that public ownership should develop everything. The only branch of public ownership that has made a great success is the one I referred to a few minutes ago.
From our experience with the other crown corporations, we know that once the house has divested itself of any control over them parliament will get no information concerning them. Kecently a list was given by one of the universities of young graduates who went to the United States. There were doctors of medicine and other professions. There were able graduates in the various branches of the great engineering profession, civil, electrical, chemical, mining, geological and other branches. They have gone to the United States to develop the resources of that country, the sea, the soil, the mines, the forests and so forth. They have gone there after this country has spent millions of dollars on their education. The provinces spend large amounts of money in grants to universities and public and separate schools to educate these young people, and when they graduate the only position they can expect in Canada, except for the odd man, is one which gives them a few dollars, not enough to keep body and soul together.
In connection with this venture I do feel that veterans should be given a chance to show what they can do in this work. Geological parties have been made up to go on surveys, and I hope that our young veterans are included. Our young Canadian university and high and technical school graduates have done much for the advancement of science, and they should be given an opportunity. The future development of the northwest territories will be somewhat under the control of the minister's department. This development may turn out to be one of the most promising that

Government Companies
we have ever had. While I have confidence in this venture and believe that it will work, still there is the question of security with regard to those who shall be employed. What check is there on these people?
Under section 8 the company is under the control and supervision of the officers and servants employed by the company. We know how it worked out with the Canadian Broadcasting corporation; they just snapped their fingers at parliament and said: "What are you going to do about it?" The same thing is true of the Canadian National railways. We have a committee that inquires into the operations of the Canadian National railways, and makes little or no check of it. On one occasion I called that committee a whitewashing committee. We do not want to have this corporation act the same way.
While I have every confidence in what is being done, I believe the time has come to limit some of the salaries to $10,000 a year. There should be a limit of $10,000 on those whom the directors employ without any order in council or special provision. I know of a young engineer about to graduate who has a position now which will pay him more than that, and he has just got a degree. That is true of the mining industry in Canada. If you pick up a copy of the manual issued by the financial and mining Companies of this country you will see what has been done there for the benefit of Canadian industry and Canadian students on whom the country has spent so much money. It is possible that in the preparatory stages we may have to bring somebody from Britain or from our neighbour to the south, but I believe that ninety-five per cent of the technical men should be Canadians who have been educated as I have indicated. If that is done we shall be giving some help toward the real development of science.
There is another bill before us which has to do with scientific and other research councils. I shall not refer to it at the moment. I do not want to see this corporation under government control turned into research, and research just to keep the government of the day in office. Parliament should have some control over it, and we should have no politics in it. It seems to me that everything in parliament is politics. We are the worst party-ridden country in the world. I say that without fear of contradiction, because I have seen something of politics, since I have been sitting on the back benches for many years. I can tell the committee that the people in the constituencies want to get value for their money, and these crown companies' are run solely from the commercial aspect. The
people do not want to see their children and their grandchildren go to the United States after having gone through our technical schools and universities in the cities where in Toronto $12 to $14 million is spent on technical education. I want to see the children and grandchildren of our soldiers of the two wars get a chance to earn a livelihood and develop their own country, for which their fathers and grandfathers fought.
We do not see much reference to this in the newspapers. We shall not see much reference to the discussion here. In fact for all we do hear we might most of the time just as well meet in secret.	_
Then we have the broadcasting corporation -another one. A motion was on the order paper to-day calling for certain information and it was challenged. The house refused to give us any information on that government corporation. There are thousands of municipalities in this country. They developed their own power through Canadian engineers. They had control because it was a municipal scheme, and there was very little politics in it. I believe the time has come to consider the scientific aspect of this matter if we are to make any headway in research. A separate research council should take control and develop and explore these subjects. We have only touched the fringe of these mining subjects in Canada. We should undertake development without politics. We should develop our great heritage, coal and all these other things. It would mean a great deal in employment to the .people of Canada. A wrong solution of it will not. If we get politics mixed up in this, we can say good-bye to any search or research, because, as I see it, that search is research trying to keep my hon. friends in office.
The minister, who is an engineer, has been showing some capacity and ability to get results. I do not agree with all that he has done, because you cannot get everybody tcf agree. Fortunately we have a diversity of opinion in this country, but I will say this about him. Since I have known him, and I have known him a long time, I have found him to be a man whom I, one of the opposition, can approach and he will give careful attention and consideration to what is placed before him. As an officer of a -municipality and chairman of the harbour board, I found that out." I do not wish to say anything further on that. This should be a non-political venture. It would be a good thing if an individual who was not known to be of a certain political stripe could be placed on the directorate. There should be included men from different branches

While I am on my feet may I say that my authorities have been questioned on the point discussed by the hon. member for Carleton. I hold in my hand the Canadian Broadcasting Act of 1936. The governor in council, on the recommendation of the minister, may authorize the Minister of Finance to place to the credit of the corporation working capital advances from any unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund, but the aggregate amount of such advances outstanding at any one time shall not exceed one hundred thousand dollars, and such advances shall be repayable to the Minister of Finance on demand.

great public service and I submit should be distinct from the commercial enterprise or enterprises upon which the government may embark under this bill. The whole realm of financial, industrial and commercial activity is thrown open to government action, and these powers will enable the government to finance these crown companies in an altogether extraordinary way. On this section several questions immediately arise. Here we have provision that the Civil Service Superannuation Act shall not apply to the officers and servants employed by any of the companies to be established under the bill. The second subsection preserves all the rights of persons who may have had any rights under the civil service superannuation provisions before becoming employees or officers of one of these crown companies. What was said yesterday as to the effect of section 8 in creating a super civil service will likewise apply to this section. Not only that, but it is quite apparent that under this section it will be possible for a number of companies-and the number is unlimited as far as the legislation is concerned-each to have its own superannuation scheme. There may be the utmost diversity as between them, with wide discrepancies in amounts. I ask if that is a sound principle.
I invite you also, Mr. Chairman, to consider the fact that when we are dealing with legislative provision for the establishment of superannuation schemes we are dealing with something that contemplates a long period of time. Let us look at this situation squarely. Actually in this legislation the minister is playing a game for 'keeps. It is not just temporary legislation; it is not legislation introduced for a temporary purpose. If that were the case there would be no occasion, I suggest, for legislative provision to establish superannuation funds and take care of employees who have given over twenty years and often a lifetime of service. Let us be quite frank about it. What the minister had to say in the first place in justification for the
bill was that there were five corporations which must continue to exist for a time, two to exist for a brief period and three for a long period.
In the two bills accompanying this bill, namely bills Nos. 154 and 165, we are asked to open the gates so that crown companies, without number and without limitation on their existence in point of time, may be established. The situation is simply this-and this section proves it beyond peradventure-that what parliament is now being asked to authorize is a permanent method of doing government business, namely a method whereby crown companies are set up by the government without first having reference to parliament, and without first having their creation subjected to direct parliamentary approval.
Legislation of this sort is not the kind of legislation which ought to precede the incorporation of crown companies to carry on specific projects of government business. If there are any hon. members who are still naive enough, after all the time spent in this debate, to believe that this is simply legislation to take care of an immediate and temporary purpose, then surely to goodness their eyes are opened by now.
I will say this for our C.C.F. friends to my left, that from the outset of the debate they have seen clearly the scope and potentialities of the bill.

. Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, the measure before us has had very full discussion and what I am about to say need not take more than a very few minutes. It has to do, however, with one of the fundamental features of the measure, namely, the drawing upon unappropriated funds for the financing of these government companies. The bill is for the operation of government companies, including their financing, and it provides for financing them out of -I think I use the words correctly-unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund.
It is important that hon. members should thoroughly understand what we are doing in this measure. The measure itself is for the operation of government companies, companies already set up under other measures, or companies which may yet be set up under measures now existing or which later may be brought in. We are saying to the government that, no matter how many of such companies there are or may be, the government by this bill may arrange for financing any or all of them from unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund.
What is the consolidated revenue fund? It is one fund into which all of the revenues of the government are brought, whether derived from taxation, from borrowings, from earnings or from any other sourcfe. That is the consolidated revenue fund. What this parliament does when the government comes in with a supply bill or a money bill or an appropriation bill is to authorize the government to spend so much money on specific enterprises of one kind or another. They are called appropriation bills. Out of that consolidated revenue fund parliament authorizes the government to draw so much money for specific purposes, nearly [DOT] -all of which will be found in the estimates for the present fiscal year and some of which will come down in supplementary estimates later.
Let us assume for a moment that the consolidated revenue fund changes. It is changing daily. Let us suppose the fund is $4,000 million, or that amount may be accumulated during a given period of time. This house may have directly authorized, either in the / estimates now or by statute formerly, the expenditure by the government of only $3,000 million. There is therefore a balance left in the consolidated revenue fund. What we are doing by this bill is saying to the government, "You have government companies now. You may set up other government companies

Government Companies
under other bills than this, and you may draw upon this fund to the extent provided for the operation of any or all of them without coming back to this house again." In other words, it is a blank cheque of a size that we do not know. Not only is it a blank cheque of a size that we do not know, but it can be arranged by the government in any way it choose after we have gone. It is in effect an appropriation bill not for this year only but for as long as the measure remains on the statute books. We thereby give the government power to draw on any balance that there may be in the consolidated revenue fund of this country, to operate these companies. My submission is that it is much too broad powers to take away from parliament and put in the hands of the governor in council. That is the only point I propose to raise on this measure at this time. I think it is a matter of fundamental concern to the house and to the country. The minister said that it had been done before in some cases. Suppose it has been. It does not need to be continued. And generally when it has been done before it has been done for specific measures. Therefore I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Boucher):
That Bill No. 155 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to committee so as to be amended as follows:
1.	That the word "unappropriated" in the third line of paragraph (a) of section 4 of the said act be deleted and the word "appropriated" be substituted in its place.
2.	That the word "unappropriated" in the second line of paragraph (b) of clause 5 of the said act be deleted and the word "appropriated" substituted in its place.
3.	That the word "unappropriated" in the third line of paragraph (c) of clause 5 of the said act be deleted and the word "appropriated" substituted in its place.
This amendment means simply that the government may draw upon funds that may be appropriated from time to time for the operation of these companies, but that we do not give the government a blank cheque now of unknown size. This bill is an appropriation measure for as long as the act remains on the statute books, the result of which is that the government may draw huge sums for the operation of present and subsequently formed companies without coming back to this house again for the appropriation of funds. The amendment I have moved would require the government to get the approval of parliament for specific expenditures. It is opposed to giving the government a blank cheque of unknown size.

I believe that one other point in the minister's last statement might be brought before the house. The minister stated that to amend the bill as suggested by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) would vitiate sections 4 and 5. Let us analyse that statement. Sections 4 and 5 provide that by order in council the dominion government may pay out of the consolidated revenue fund to any crown company and any number of crown companies a sum or sums up to $500,000, and at any time. In the second place, it can give in the same way to any company or any number of companies, and even the same company or companies as before, in any fiscal year and, I submit, in every fiscal year if that should be so decided, a further sum of $500,000. The minister says that even if an order in council is passed allocating moneys to these firms it will be brought back to parliament and there discussed. I cannot agree with that statement because I do not understand how it would be done. This amendment simply means that the money must be voted by parliament before an order in council can transfer it to a company.
The minister says that if the government is not permitted to advance this money by order in council before it is voted by parliament, sections 4 and 5 are of no value, that their meaning will be destroyed. According to his statement, therefore, sections 4 and 5 have absolutely no meaning or significance if

Government Companies
parliament is consulted before an order in council is passed. But he suggests they have a meaning if the order in council can be passed giving the money to the companies, with parliament then asked to approve something already accomplished. In other words parliament is to be asked to lock the barn door after the horse is stolen. I believe that the minister's own statement more than justifies the discussion this afternoon and last evening in opposition to this blank cheque legislation. I say "blank cheque" because, while it is a limited cheque, there is no limit to the number of companies that may get this limited cheque, or on the number of years during which that cheque may be issued.
In the amendment which was moved before the bill came out of committee the minister said he was making this act apply to one company; that they could not make it apply to any others, but they could make it apply to any company by order in council at any time they saw fit to do so. In view of these very revealing statements by the minister, Mr. Speaker, I believe the present amendment is entirely justified.

Mr. Speaker, this is the end product of what I referred to last evening. During yesterday's debate most of the hon. gentlemen to my right who spoke to this measure referred to the few remarks I made the previous evenings Of course I feel greatly flattered that what I said should have so much significance, but as a matter of fact I did not say at all what my hon. friends have suggested I did. We are supporting this bill, not because it represents socialism or is a step in that direction. I am not going to discuss that aspect now, but I want to submit that in my opinion the amendment is out of order. I would refer to citation 344 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, at page 136:
It is an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed. Every amendment proposed to be made either to a question or to a proposed amendment should be so framed that if agreed to by the house the question or amendment as amended would be intelligible and consistent with itself.
I submit, sir, that this amendment is not intelligible or consistent with itself. Tlae leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) movea the amendment and then explained it; but what he said in explanation is not what the house has before it. It has what appears in the written amendment, and it contains these words:
That Bill No. 155 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to committee so as to be amended as follows:
1.	That the word "unappropriated" in the third line of paragraph (a) of section 4 of the said act be deleted and the word "appropriated" be substituted in its place.
Then it goes on through the other sections, proposing a similar change. The point I wish to make is that if the money has already been appropriated it cannot be appropriated a second time. Consequently I submit that the amendment is out of order.
